raw_response:
I've farmed this land in Quzhou my whole life. The North China Plain gives us one reliable system: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same plots. I'm not changing that — it's what the market wants, what the land supports, and what I know how to do well.

I have 8 mu of arable land. The wheat goes in around mid-October; I harvest it in early June. Then I plant maize immediately — no-till, right into the stubble — and harvest in late September. Same 8 mu, two crops per year.

For wheat, I'll buy certified improved seed from the county station — probably Hengguan 35 or whatever the extension office is recommending this year for disease resistance. Hybrid wheat isn't standard here and the seed cost isn't worth it. For maize, hybrid is the only choice that makes sense for yield — I'll use Xianyu 335 or Zhengdan 958.

On fertilizer, I had my soil tested two years ago and I follow those numbers closely. I'm not a heavy hand with nitrogen — I've seen neighbors burn crops and waste money. I split my nitrogen on wheat: base dressing at planting, then topdress at jointing.

On irrigation: I'm doing three waterings for wheat, not four. I skip the wintering irrigation. The groundwater table has dropped noticeably in the past ten years and I feel responsible for that. Summer maize mostly runs on rainfall here — one irrigation at silking if July is dry.

Pesticide: seed treatment counts as one application. I spray herbicide in early spring for wheat, then a fungicide at heading. For maize, one herbicide pass after emergence, and I watch for corn borer but usually don't need a second application.
